newsitem.title: USA: NEW PRODUCTS - Andyroo Tapes developed to aid children at bedtime.
newsitem.headline: NEW PRODUCTS - Andyroo Tapes developed to aid children at bedtime.

text.p: Like many toddlers, Andrew would rather take in the world than settle down for a night's sleep. He was happy as a clam laughing and chattering to all hours, but his parents needed some rest.

His mother, Paige Latta, found that story telling at nap or bed time kept him up and music didn't seem to soothe him. Videos of cartoons were often very scary and the long story plots didn't hold the attention of a very small child.
So Latta, a writer, made up her own very short scenes for Andrew.
"I tried to develop his vocabulary, imagination and senses all at once, telling him stories that were very descriptive," she said from her home in Delray Beach, Fla.

However, after telling the same stories for the umpteenth time, she admitedly got tired. Latta recorded Andrew's favourite stories along with sleep tapes of waterfalls and jungle sounds on her karaoke machine. Thus, she came up with a failsafe method to get her son, now 7, to sleep.
Andyroo Dream Tapes were born out of necessity -- which is in this case indeed the mother of invention.
Latta said Andrew's sleep problem is not unusual, calling it "the No. 1 problem with moms."
Informally, Latta gave copies of the audio cassette tapes to friends who encouraged her to go ahead on a larger, more professional scale.
The trick, she said, is to keep the stories on the tapes very simple. They run for 15 minutes, then meld into the related sounds, which run for an additional 15 minutes.
"We did a lot of reading on this, and no one has hit upon the idea of combining story and sounds," she said.
First, the tape captures the child's attention. It's not quiet and soft. "It grabs the child so he'll be interested in the tape not in Mommy walking out of the room."
Then it slows down gradually and moves into the soothing sounds for the final 15 minutes.

The first set of tapes, which were completed in January, include four stories -- Andyroo goes to the beach; Andyroo goes to the farm; Grandma and Grandpa go for a ride in the car; and Tiger's surpise birthday.
"We want every child to identify with Andyroo so we don't describe the child except that he has big brown eyes and curly hair," she said.
This allows each child to develop his own sense of what the character looks like and helps develop his imagination and sense of "a story world."

The Andyroo Dream Tapes are appropriate for children ages two to seven, depending on the child, Latta said. While each child might react to the tapes differently, "if they're not asleep at the end of the 30 minutes, forget it."
Latta said her own mother konked out before the end of a tape.
The tapes were made in a Ft. Lauderdale recording studio (which has done some work with Jimmy Buffett, Latta said) and uses Delray Beach's children's librarian, Lynda Hunter, as narrator
Paige and husband John, a freelance writer, are planning to produce two more sets of tapes and a special Christmas set, if possible.

A set of two tapes, with four stories, sells for $12.99 plus $2.50 for shipping and handling. For more information, call 1-800-707-8449, or write The Andyroo Company, PO Box 1766, Delray Beach, Fla. 33447. The e-mail address is Andyroo(at)aol.com.
Here's another new product hitting the market:

Healthy Choice, a division of Con Agra Inc., has teamed up with Tanimura & Antle, the largest independent U.S. lettuce grower, to develop Healthy Choice Salad Bar Select -- pre-cut, packaged fresh salad mixes.
There will be six fresh-cut bagged salads and six single-serve salads. Salad toppings include three diced meats, three shredded cheeses, four dressings and three toppings.
The products are being introduced currently in the Phoenix/Tucson market. Additional rollouts have not been announced. Prices are not yet available.
